In this Section, we introduce three versions of the MultiZenoTravel problem: the symmetric clique
MultiZenoTravel, the non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel and the general MultiZenoTravel. We then
make precise what a plan is, together with its cost and its makespan, and the assumptions on
durations used in the rest of the paper. Plans are defined flight by flight, with explicit
departure times, so that waiting, passengers changing planes, empty flights and flights between
central cities are part of the problem and not excluded by assumption. The characterization of the
Pareto-optimal plans comes next: for the [symmetric clique problem](front.qmd) first, then for the
[non-symmetric and general problems](nonsymmetric.qmd).

## Instances {#sec-instances}

Let us introduce some notations related to the planning problem briefly presented in the
introduction: a non-symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel instance
([schematic view](index.qmd#fig-instance)) is defined by the following elements
({{< node "§1.1" >}}):

* $n$ central cities, organized as a clique in which every node is connected to $C_I$ and $C_G$,
  respectively the initial city and the goal city.
* $c \in (\mathbb R^+)^n$, where $c_i$ is the cost for landing in $C_i$.
* $D \in (\mathbb R^+)^{n \times n}$, where $d_{ij}$ is the flying time between $C_i$ and $C_j$.
* $d \in (\mathbb R^+)^n$, where $d_i$ is the flying time between $C_I$ and $C_i$.
* $\bar d \in (\mathbb R^+)^n$, where $\bar d_i$ is the flying time between $C_i$ and $C_G$.
* $p$ planes, initially in $C_I$, that have a capacity of a unique person.
* $t$ persons, initially in $C_I$.

The goal of MultiZenoTravel is to carry all $t$ persons, initially in $C_I$, to $C_G$ using $p$
planes, minimizing both the makespan and the cost of the plan.

Flights are undirected: each one has a single duration, used in both directions, and there is no
flight between $C_I$ and $C_G$. We write $\mathrm{dur}(a, b)$ for the duration of the flight
between $a$ and $b$; a flight between central cities may also be missing. Landing in $C_I$ or
$C_G$ is free. Without loss of generality, all triples $(d_i, \bar d_i, c_i)$ are assumed to be
pairwise distinct. Otherwise, the 2 cities can be "merged" and the resulting $n-1$ cities problem
is equivalent to the original $n$ cities problem, as there exist no city capacity constraints.
Finally, we only consider cases where $t \ge p$, as the problem is otherwise trivial.

An instance of the symmetric clique MultiZenoTravel problem is an instance such that
$d = \bar d$. A general MultiZenoTravel instance is an instance such that the $n$ central cities
are organized as an arbitrary graph; it is defined in the
[general section](nonsymmetric.qmd#sec-graphs).

Throughout the paper, we illustrate the definitions on the symmetric instance with $n = 3$
cities, $t = 3$ passengers and $p = 2$ planes, durations $d = (2, 3, 5)$, costs
$c = (9, 6, 1)$ and no flight between central cities (the file
[`site/problem/example.dat`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/site/problem/example.dat),
also used on the [Problem](../problem.qmd) page). Its Pareto front, as (cost, makespan), is
$$(4, 20),\ (14, 16),\ (20, 14),\ (24, 12),\ (30, 10),\ (36, 8).$$

::: {#fig-plan .plan-display}

$$
\begin{array}{lllllll}
p_1: & C_I & \overset{t_1}{\to} C_2 & \to C_I & \overset{t_2}{\to} C_3 & \overset{t_2}{\to} C_G & \\
p_2: & C_I & \overset{t_3}{\to} C_3 & \overset{t_3}{\to} C_G & \to C_2 & \overset{t_1}{\to} C_G &
\end{array}
$$

Example of an admissible plan to transport 3 travelers via 2 planes, on the instance above. This
representation indicates the successive actions for each plane. We noted by
$\overset{t_i}{\to}$ a flight with a traveler.
:::

@fig-plan illustrates an admissible solution, of cost 14 and makespan 16. Note that the makespan
for a plan is not necessarily the largest sum of the flights' duration as some planes might have
to wait for others. This would be the case for $p_2$ waiting for $t_1$ in $C_2$, had it reached
$C_2$ before $p_1$ dropped $t_1$ there.

## Plans {#sec-plans}

To reason about all plans, including those that wait, hand passengers over or fly between
central cities, we fix their semantics ({{< node "§1.2" >}}). A plan on a set $Q$ of planes (all
$p$ planes unless stated otherwise) consists of

1. for every plane $k \in Q$, a *route*: a sequence of *legs* $(k, 1), \dots, (k, \nu_k)$. Leg
   $(k, j)$ flies an existing flight from $v_{k,j-1}$ to $v_{k,j}$ and departs at time
   $e_{k,j}$, with $v_{k,0} = C_I$, $e_{k,1} \ge 0$, and
   $e_{k,j+1} \ge a_{k,j} := e_{k,j} + \mathrm{dur}(v_{k,j-1}, v_{k,j})$;
2. for every passenger, a *journey*: a non-empty sequence of legs whose first leg departs from
   $C_I$ and whose last leg arrives in $C_G$. Each leg departs from the city where the previous
   one arrives, no earlier than that arrival, and, if both legs belong to the same plane, at a
   later position of its route;
3. *capacity*: the journeys are pairwise disjoint, and none repeats a leg.

The plan is *feasible* if every route ends in $C_G$. Its *cost* $C$ is the sum of the landing
costs of all legs, with or without a passenger, and its *makespan* $M = \max_k a_{k,\nu_k}$ is
the time at which the last plane reaches $C_G$ for the last time. $\mathcal A$ is the set of
pairs $(C, M)$ of feasible plans. The *flight time* $F_k$ of plane $k$ is the sum of the
durations of its legs; its flights are sequential, so $F_k \le M$.

Waiting is implicit: a plane or a passenger may depart later than it arrived. Boarding and
deplaning take no time, several planes may be in a city at once, and a passenger may change
planes in any city, any number of times. In @fig-plan, $t_1$ changes planes once, in $C_2$.

Journeys may contain detours that serve nothing, and they can be removed:

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 3.1" >}} **Cleaning.** Every plan can be changed, keeping all routes (hence its
cost, makespan and flight times), so that every journey is *clean*: its first flight is its only
flight departing from $C_I$, and its last flight is its only flight arriving in $C_G$.
:::

::: {.sketch}
*Sketch.* Cut each journey down to the part from its last departure from $C_I$ to the first later
arrival in $C_G$; this is still a journey, and capacity only gets looser
({{< node "Lemma 3.1" text="full proof" badge=false >}}).
:::

A plan is *event-ordered* if its legs admit a total order that extends every route and every
journey and along which departure times do not decrease. With positive durations every plan is
event-ordered. With zero durations, a passenger can ride a later leg of one plane and then an
earlier leg of another at the same instant, in a cycle that no execution in time realises; such
plans never improve the front ({{< node "Corollary 6.10" >}}).

Requiring planes to finish in $C_G$ does not change the front: if planes may end anywhere, with
the makespan taken as the last arrival of any leg, the Pareto front is the same under the
assumptions of the next section ({{< node "Theorem 4.9" >}}). All the planes may thus be assumed
to finish their respective sequence in $C_G$.

ZenoSolver outputs each instance as a PDDL file[^pddl] for the domain
[`pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl`](https://github.com/aquemy/ZenoSolver/blob/master/pddl/multi-zeno-travel.pddl):
a durative `fly` action that adds the landing cost to `total-cost`, instantaneous `board` and
`debark` actions, and a predicate `libre` that enforces capacity one. Under
$\varepsilon$-separation, PDDL plans and event-ordered plans correspond, with the same cost and
makespans equal in the limit $\varepsilon \to 0$ ({{< node "Statement 1.2" >}}); this
correspondence is argued but not formalised. The [Instances](../instances/index.qmd) section
describes the generator and the files.

[^pddl]: Planning Domain Definition Language [[FL03](index.qmd#ref-FL03)], almost universally used
in AI Planning to describe domains and instances.

## Pareto fronts {#sec-fronts}

For points $y, z$ of the plane (cost, makespan), $y \preceq z$ if $y \le z$ in both coordinates.
For a set $\mathcal S$ of points, $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$ is the set of $z \in \mathcal S$
weakly dominated by no other point of $\mathcal S$, and the *Pareto front* of an instance is
$\mathcal F = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal A$ ({{< node "§1.5" >}}). We look for the front and for one
plan per front point.

Every characterization of the front in this paper has two halves: a finite set of points that
plans attain, and a proof that every plan is weakly dominated by one of them. The following lemma
turns them into an equality of fronts.

::: {.statement}
{{< node "Lemma 1.1" >}} **Dominating subset.** Let $\mathcal S' \subseteq \mathcal S$ with
$\mathcal S'$ finite and every point of $\mathcal S$ weakly dominated by a point of
$\mathcal S'$. Then $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S = \mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S'$, and every point of
$\mathcal S$ is weakly dominated by a point of $\mathrm{Min}\,\mathcal S$.
:::

## Assumptions {#sec-assumptions}

The results of this paper use the following assumptions ({{< node "§1.4" >}}), each one only
where stated. The first two are the triangular inequality and the symmetry assumption:

**Assumption**: $\forall (a, b, x),\ \mathrm{dur}(a, x) + \mathrm{dur}(x, b) \ge \mathrm{dur}(a, b)$
whenever the three flights exist $\hfill$ (AΔ)

**Assumption** (Symmetry): $\forall i \in [1, n],\ d_i = \bar d_i$ $\hfill$ (S)

The assumption of [[QS15](index.qmd#ref-QS15)], in a non-strict form, and its non-symmetric
counterpart state that flights between central cities are useless, that is, never faster than a
detour through $C_I$ or $C_G$:

**Assumption**: under (S), $\forall (i, j),\ d_{ij} \ge d_i + d_j$ for every existing flight
$\hfill$ (A1)

**Assumption**: $\forall (i, j),\ d_{ij} \ge \min(d_i + d_j,\ \bar d_i + \bar d_j)$ for every
existing flight $\hfill$ (A1-NS)

Finally, a weak form of the triangular inequality through the hubs is used for waiting:

**Assumption**: $\forall (i, z),\ \bar d_i \le d_i + d_z + \bar d_z$ and
$d_i \le \bar d_i + \bar d_z + d_z$ $\hfill$ (AΔ-path)

(S) implies (AΔ-path), and so does (AΔ) whenever the flight between $i$ and $z$ exists. Under
(S), (A1) and (AΔ) hold together only when $d_{ij} = d_i + d_j$: the first allows flights
between central cities longer than the detour through a hub, and the second allows them as short
as $|d_i - d_j|$. Every PDDL problem the generator writes is symmetric, and gives a flight between
central cities the duration $d_i + d_j + 100$, so it satisfies (A1).

**Notation.** We write $s = 2t - p$, so that $s \ge p$ and $s \equiv p \pmod 2$, and
$\kappa = \lceil s/p \rceil$ ({{< node "Notation" >}}). For a multiset $Y$ of central cities,
$Y(i)$ is the multiplicity of $i$, $|Y|$ its size, $c(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} c_w$ its cost, and
$\delta(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} d_w$ and $\bar\delta(Y) = \sum_{w \in Y} \bar d_w$ its durations;
under (S), its *load* is $\ell(Y) = 2\delta(Y)$. A *partition* of $X$ over the planes is a family
of groups $X_1, \dots, X_p$ with $X_1 + \dots + X_p = X$, group $X_k$ being the cities in which
plane $k$ lands.

## Patterns {#sec-patterns}

Cut the sequence of a plane at every visit to $C_I$ or $C_G$. Each piece, from one of them to the
next, is a *pattern* (a *segment* in the [blueprint](../proofs.qmd)). As there is no flight
between $C_I$ and $C_G$, every pattern lands in at least one central city. Depending on the
cities it starts and ends in, a pattern is of one of four types, denoted by $A$, $\bar A$, $B$ and
$\bar B$ (@fig-patterns). A pattern that lands in exactly one central city, of *multiplicity*
0, consists of two flights; we call it *simple*. We denote by $|X|$ the number of the patterns
$X \in \{A, \bar A, B, \bar B\}$ in a given plan, and by $F(\gamma)$ the flight time of a
pattern $\gamma$.

::: {#fig-patterns}

The simple patterns $A$, $\bar A$, $B$ and $\bar B$, with $I = C_I$ and $G = C_G$. In the plans
built in this paper, a pattern $A$ carries a passenger from $C_I$ to $C_G$, a pattern $\bar A$
flies back empty, a pattern $B$ leaves a passenger in $x$ and a pattern $\bar B$ takes one from
$x$ to $C_G$. Patterns of larger multiplicity have the same four types.
:::

In @fig-plan, $p_1$ performs a $B$ in $C_2$ and an $A$ in $C_3$, and $p_2$ an $A$ in $C_3$ and a
$\bar B$ in $C_2$. Only the patterns $A$ and $\bar A$ change from $C_I$ to $C_G$ or back, and a
plane goes from $C_I$ to $C_G$, so its patterns of these two types alternate $A, \bar A, \dots, A$
({{< node "Lemma 2.1" >}}). We deduce the following property on the cardinal of each pattern in
any feasible plan.

**Property II**: In every feasible plan,

1. $|A| + |B| \ge t$;
2. $|A| + |\bar B| \ge t$;
3. $|A| = |\bar A| + p$.

**Proof**: The patterns $A$ and $B$ are the only ones that start with a flight from $C_I$, and
the first flights of the journeys are distinct flights from $C_I$, so a feasible plan has at least
$t$ of those patterns. Apply the same reasoning to $C_G$ with $A$ and $\bar B$, whose last flight
arrives in $C_G$, to prove the second point. The third point is Lemma 2.1, summed over the $p$
planes. $\square$

**Corollary II**: A feasible plan performs at least $2t - p$ patterns, hence lands at least
$2t - p$ times in central cities ({{< node "Lemma 3.2" >}}).

**Proof**: By Property II, the number of patterns is
$|A| + |\bar A| + |B| + |\bar B| = (|A| + |B|) + (|A| + |\bar B|) - p \ge 2t - p$, and each
pattern lands in a central city. $\square$

With fewer planes than passengers, some planes have to come back to $C_I$, and every return costs
a landing. In @fig-plan the bound is reached: the plan lands $2t - p = 4$ times. The
[next section](front.qmd) shows that, in the symmetric case, the Pareto front is always reached
by such plans, and which lists of $2t - p$ cities can be flown, and how fast.
